Family Health

Painful urination: causes, treatment and when to seek care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pain or burning when passing urine is called dysuria. It is a symptom with several possible causes, rather than a diagnosis you can establish from the sensation alone. A urinary tract infection is common, but genital irritation, sexually transmitted infections, stones and other conditions can feel similar. The safest plan starts with the cause and how unwell you feel.

What painful urination can feel like

Discomfort may be felt at the urine opening, along the urethra, in the bladder area or around the perineum: the area between the anus and genitals. Notice whether it happens before, during or after urination, and whether you also have urgency, frequent trips, a weak stream or difficulty emptying.

The kidneys make urine, the ureters carry it to the bladder and the urethra takes it out of the body. Irritation or infection in this system, or soreness of nearby genital tissue, can cause burning. The location alone does not reliably identify the cause.

When to seek prompt or emergency help

Arrange assessment for persistent or recurring pain, genital discharge, or new abdominal, pelvic or back pain. Get urgent same-day advice for visible or suspected blood in urine, even if it happens only once, is a small amount or you are unsure it is blood. Get prompt same-day advice for suspected infection during pregnancy, fever or shaking chills, vomiting, flank pain, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Children, older frail adults, people with a prostate, diabetes, a catheter or reduced immunity may need earlier assessment.

Seek emergency care if you cannot pass urine, especially with a painful or swollen lower abdomen, have sudden severe testicular pain, severe pelvic pain with fainting or heavy bleeding, or become confused, very drowsy or seriously short of breath. Infection, obstruction, testicular torsion and pregnancy-related emergencies need consideration. Do not wait for a home remedy or assume these are ordinary cystitis.

Urinary tract infection and why anatomy matters

A bladder infection often causes burning, urgency and frequent small amounts of urine, sometimes with lower abdominal discomfort. Most bladder infections are bacterial. Cloudiness or an unusual smell can accompany infection, but smell or dark urine alone can also reflect concentration and does not prove a UTI. Fever, chills, nausea or back/side pain may suggest infection involving a kidney.

A shorter urethra makes it easier for bacteria to reach the bladder, so infections occur more often in people with female urinary anatomy. Pregnancy and menopausal changes can also change risk or management. Repeated symptoms still need assessment; not every episode of burning in a woman is a bacterial infection.

Sexually transmitted infection and urethritis

Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and genital herpes can cause painful urination. Discharge, genital sores or recent exposure may guide testing, but an STI can occur without obvious symptoms. Ask about appropriate testing based on your symptoms, sexual history and local recommendations rather than assuming that no discharge means no infection.

Urethritis means inflammation of the urethra; it is different from arthritis, which affects joints. It can follow an STI or noninfectious irritation. Treatment depends on the cause. If an STI is diagnosed, follow advice about partner testing and treatment, and when sex can safely resume; condoms reduce risk but do not provide absolute protection.

Prostate and epididymis problems

Prostatitis can cause burning, difficulty urinating, pelvic or genital pain and pain with ejaculation; fever can occur. A prostate problem is one possible explanation, not the answer to every episode in a man. Acute infection and long-lasting pelvic pain require different assessments and may need different treatment.

Epididymitis affects the sperm-carrying tube behind a testicle. Pain or swelling of the scrotum can accompany urinary symptoms or discharge, sometimes because of an STI or urinary infection. Sudden severe testicular pain is an emergency because a twisted testicle can look similar; do not diagnose epididymitis yourself or wait for antibiotics to work.

Bladder pain, interstitial cystitis and radiation

Cystitis means bladder inflammation and is often associated with a bacterial infection. Interstitial cystitis, also called bladder pain syndrome, is a distinct long-lasting condition with bladder or pelvic discomfort and urinary frequency or urgency. Pain often increases as the bladder fills and eases after urination. It should not be described as the most common form of cystitis.

Symptoms can overlap, so a clinician assesses infection and other explanations before deciding on a bladder-pain diagnosis. Pelvic radiotherapy can separately irritate the bladder lining and cause radiation cystitis. Tell the care team about previous or current radiation treatment, particularly if there is bleeding or trouble emptying the bladder.

Pelvic inflammatory disease and genital soreness

Infection affecting the uterus, fallopian tubes or ovaries is called pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Pelvic pain, pain during sex, unusual discharge or bleeding may occur, sometimes alongside urinary discomfort. It needs prompt assessment and treatment; severe pain, faintness or possible pregnancy makes the situation more urgent. Vaginal or vulval inflammation, including yeast infection or menopausal tissue changes, can also sting when urine touches sore tissue and needs a different approach from a bladder infection.

Stones, narrowing and blocked urine flow

Kidney stones are hard deposits formed from substances in urine. They can cause severe side or back pain spreading toward the groin, blood in the urine or urinary symptoms. Fever with suspected stones is particularly concerning. The size, position, infection risk and ability to pass urine determine treatment; not every stone passes safely without help.

Narrowing of the urethra or another blockage can interfere with emptying, cause a weak stream or lead to urine retention. Obstruction elsewhere in the urinary tract can put pressure on the kidneys. Difficulty passing urine deserves assessment; complete inability with pain requires urgent emergency care, rather than drinking more water and waiting.

Medicines and products that irritate

Some cancer medicines and pelvic cancer treatments can affect the bladder or kidneys. Report new urinary pain to the treatment team promptly. If symptoms began after any new medicine, including an antibiotic, ask the prescriber about the timing and possible causes. Do not assume the drug is responsible or stop necessary treatment yourself.

Perfumed soaps, bubble baths, lotions, detergents and other products can irritate genital tissue. Stop a suspected irritating cosmetic product and use gentle care, but seek assessment if pain persists or infection symptoms are present. Irritation and infection can coexist; removing a product does not exclude another cause.

What the appointment and tests may involve

Describe the duration and timing of pain, urine frequency or flow, fever, bleeding, genital symptoms, recent sex, pregnancy possibility, previous stones and medicines. A clinician may examine the abdomen or genital area and ask about relevant prostate or pelvic symptoms. You can ask for an explanation and support during an examination.

A urine sample, culture or STI tests may help, depending on the situation. Pregnancy testing, blood tests or imaging may be appropriate when symptoms suggest pregnancy-related problems, stones, obstruction or a more serious infection. Not everyone needs every test, and persistent symptoms after treatment deserve reassessment even if an initial result was reassuring.

Treatment follows the cause, not just the burning

Antibiotics can treat a bacterial UTI and certain bacterial STIs; they do not treat every cause of dysuria or genital herpes. Use only the treatment prescribed for the diagnosis, follow its instructions and do not share or use leftover antibiotics. Seek review if symptoms worsen or do not begin improving within the time your clinician specified; for a treated UTI, lack of improvement after about 48 hours is a reason to contact the service.

Pain relief may be useful when suitable for your health and pregnancy status. Stones, obstruction, irritation and chronic bladder pain each need a tailored plan. Interstitial cystitis may involve lifestyle changes, pelvic-floor therapy, medicines or other specialist treatment, sometimes with trials of several options. There is no reliable universal four-month treatment limit or guaranteed cure.

Comfort measures and reducing future risk

Drink an appropriate amount of fluid to avoid dehydration, unless your clinician has advised a restriction. Do not force large volumes if you cannot urinate. Avoid fragranced genital products and consider whether a detergent causes irritation. Coffee, alcohol or acidic drinks can aggravate symptoms for some people; a symptom diary can identify personal triggers without unnecessary blanket food restrictions.

Safer sex and correctly used condoms can lower the risk of some infections. If infection is suspected or diagnosed, obtain specific advice on testing, treatment and avoiding transmission. Water, dietary changes and cranberry products cannot replace assessment or treat an established infection. A symptom record may help the appointment, but it cannot determine the diagnosis.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS, NIDDK and MedlinePlus distinguish common infections from other causes and support assessment based on accompanying symptoms.

Urethritis, prostate, epididymal and pelvic conditions require the appropriate tests and treatment; urinary pain alone does not diagnose them.

NIDDK describes interstitial cystitis as a chronic condition with individualized treatment and no single fixed treatment course.

Cancer-treatment urinary effects and radiation cystitis were checked against NCI information; new symptoms should be reported to the treating team.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note symptom timing, urine changes, medicines and questions. These notes can support an appointment; they do not diagnose an infection, rule out pregnancy complications or decide which medicine you need.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for pregnancy, fever, flank pain, visible blood, discharge, worsening or persistent symptoms. Inability to pass urine with pain, sudden severe testicular pain, severe pelvic pain with fainting or heavy bleeding, confusion or serious breathlessness needs emergency care. This article is general education and does not replace individual assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Burning is a symptom; infection, irritation, stones and other conditions need different treatment.
  • Pregnancy, fever, flank pain, blood or worsening symptoms require prompt advice.
  • Inability to pass urine, especially with pain, or sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency assessment.
  • Do not assume every episode needs antibiotics or stop a necessary medicine yourself.
  • Persistent symptoms deserve review; home comfort measures do not establish or cure the cause.

Frequently asked questions

Why does painful urination recur more often in women?

A shorter urethra helps bacteria reach the bladder, and pregnancy or menopausal changes can affect risk. Recurrent burning may have other causes too, so repeated symptoms need review.

Can it be related to the prostate?

Yes. Prostatitis can cause burning and pelvic or genital symptoms, but infection, stones, irritation and other problems are also possible. Seek assessment rather than assuming a prostate diagnosis.

Can a pelvic infection cause urinary discomfort?

PID can occur with pelvic pain, painful sex or unusual discharge and sometimes urinary symptoms. It needs prompt clinical assessment; severe pain, fainting or possible pregnancy increases urgency.

Could a medicine be responsible?

Some treatments, especially certain cancer therapies, can irritate the urinary tract. Tell the prescriber about a new symptom and all medicines you take; do not independently stop treatment or presume causation.

Does burning always mean I need antibiotics?

No. Antibiotics are useful for selected bacterial infections, not all irritation, bladder pain, stones or viral infection. The treatment depends on the assessment.

Is urethritis a type of arthritis?

No. Urethritis affects the tube carrying urine out; arthritis affects joints. Urethritis may be infectious or caused by irritation.

Can I wait during pregnancy?

Contact your maternity or medical service promptly for painful urination or suspected UTI during pregnancy. Fever, flank pain, vomiting or feeling very unwell increases urgency; home measures should not delay care.

When is emergency care needed?

Examples include inability to pass urine, especially with a painful lower abdomen, sudden severe testicular pain, severe pelvic pain with fainting or heavy bleeding, confusion or serious breathing difficulty. Use local emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
